title: Intel Shares Plummet, Erasing $12 B from Government Stake – TechCrunch Reports
body:
Intel’s shares plunged nearly 28% on Friday, delivering one of the sharpest single‑day drops in the company’s history and wiping roughly $12 billion from the value of the U.S. government’s equity stake in the chipmaker. The slide followed Intel’s release of a fourth‑quarter outlook that fell short of analysts’ expectations, underscoring how a slowdown in personal‑computer demand and an escalating competition for memory and other components in the fast‑growing artificial‑intelligence (AI) sector are straining the traditional semiconductor powerhouse.

The market reaction was swift and severe. By the close of trading, Intel’s stock was down $15.3 billion in market capitalization, leaving the company’s valuation at its lowest point since early 2022. The decline came despite the firm’s robust earnings in the preceding quarters, which had been buoyed by a resurgence in data‑center sales and a series of strategic acquisitions aimed at expanding its AI‑focused product line. Analysts cited the guidance for Q4 revenue—projected at $12.5 billion to $13.5 billion, well below the consensus estimate of $13.9 billion—as the primary catalyst for the sell‑off, noting that the outlook signaled a broader weakness in the PC market that still accounts for a sizable share of Intel’s revenue.

The PC segment, once the engine of Intel’s growth, is now feeling the pressure of a shifting technology landscape. As AI workloads demand ever‑larger memory capacities and specialized accelerators, manufacturers of graphics processing units and high‑bandwidth memory are seeing unprecedented demand, driving up component prices and squeezing profit margins for downstream PC makers. Higher component costs have translated into elevated retail prices for laptops and desktops, dampening consumer demand at a time when many households are still recovering from pandemic‑induced spending spikes. Intel, whose business model relies heavily on supplying CPUs for a wide range of personal computers, is consequently seeing a dip in orders, a trend that appears to be persisting into the current fiscal year.

The impact extends beyond the private sector. The U.S. Treasury, which holds a $12 billion stake in Intel through various sovereign wealth and pension funds, saw the value of that investment erode dramatically in a single trading session. While the loss is unlikely to affect the Treasury’s overall balance sheet, it highlights the broader financial risk that government‑linked holdings face when tied to volatile technology stocks. Some policymakers have already begun discussing whether greater diversification of public‑sector portfolios could mitigate such exposure, especially as the semiconductor industry becomes increasingly cyclical and susceptible to rapid shifts in demand.

Industry observers also pointed to Intel’s ongoing transition to a “foundry” model, where the company intends to manufacture chips for external customers in addition to its own products. The strategic pivot, announced last year, aims to capture a share of the lucrative AI chip market dominated by rivals such as NVIDIA and AMD. However, the execution timeline has encountered setbacks, including delays in the rollout of its latest 7‑nanometer process node and supply‑chain bottlenecks that have hampered capacity expansion. The weaker outlook suggests that the company’s internal challenges may be delaying the anticipated revenue boost from its foundry services, further unsettling investors.

Looking ahead, Intel’s leadership has signaled a commitment to address the shortfall by accelerating its roadmap for next‑generation processors and expanding partnerships with AI developers. The firm is also expected to unveil additional cost‑reduction initiatives aimed at restoring confidence among PC OEMs. Market participants will be watching closely for any updates on the company’s progress in bringing its new “Meteor Lake” and “Arrow Lake” architectures to market, as well as the pace at which its foundry business can secure high‑margin contracts. If Intel can successfully navigate the current headwinds and capitalize on the burgeoning AI demand, the recent plunge could be a temporary setback; if not, the stock may remain under pressure, prompting investors to reassess the chipmaker’s long‑term growth narrative.
